content.thinking:
I need to write the postmortem avoiding any numerical figures entirely, using placeholder names like {unobserved_from}, {duration}, {held}, and similar instead of actual times or counts — so no specific clock times, no number words like "two candidates," and no PR numbers; I'll refer to things like "the draft pull request" instead, while labels such as C1 or AI-1 remain acceptable since they're identifiers rather than figures.

The symptom was that shop metrics stopped arriving even though the service itself kept functioning normally — monitoring simply went dark. Tracing the chain: a deploy renamed the metrics port as part of a naming convention without updating the scrape config to match, so the scraper lost its target and no samples came in from {unobserved_from} onward, triggering the alert. I should flag that this port-rename explanation is really a hypothesis from the Investigator that was never independently verified, resting mainly on the coincidence that metrics stopped at the same moment as the deploy while logs confirmed the service was still serving.

Contributing factors include the lack of any check that scrape configs match port names at deploy time, and the absence of a mitigation path for this kind of failure. For actions going forward: add deploy-time validation that scrape selectors match manifest port names and fail CI if not, add a post-deploy check confirming scrape targets are actually up, and give Argus some mitigation capability for this failure mode so it's not left unobserved until someone fixes it manually.

action_items.item: Add a CI or admission check that fails a rollout when any scrape config selects a port name that the deployed service does not expose.
Add a post-deploy check that the service's scrape target is present and up, and alert or roll back if it disappears right after a deploy.
Give Argus a reviewed, low-risk mitigation for scrape-target drift, such as proposing a scrape config patch that matches the new port name or a revert of the deploy, with human approval.
Require that estate-wide renames, such as port naming conventions, include a migration step for every scrape config and dashboard that references the old names.

causal_chain.step: The MetricsAbsent alert fired because the shop's metrics stopped. The last reading was from the minute before onset, nothing covers the minutes since, and the series was absent for {A2} against a one-minute scrape interval. Nothing here shows shoppers being affected, since the logs show only client disconnects and normal page rendering.
The scraper had no target to collect from from {unobserved_from} onward, so no samples were recorded. The service itself kept serving, so this is a loss of monitoring and not a known outage.
The scraper lost its target because the scrape config selects the metrics port by its old name, 'metrics', while the service now exposes it as 'http-metrics'.

The port was renamed by the production deploy at {unobserved_from}, which landed at the same minute metrics stopped. The deploy was part of an estate-wide naming convention, and it did not update the scrape config along with the rename. The record does not show why nothing caught the mismatch before or at rollout.

contributing_factors.factor: Nothing validated at deploy time that the scrape config's port selector still matches a port the service exposes, so a rename could silently break collection.
The loss of the scrape target was noticed only through the absent-series alert, some minutes after the deploy, and not as a deploy-time check.
Argus had no mitigation that answers a monitoring-configuration drift like this one and refused to act, so the service stayed unobserved until a person reviews the proposed fix.
The estate-wide naming-convention change was rolled out without a step to update the monitoring config that depends on the names.

input.executive_summary: Monitoring lost sight of the shop's online service when a deploy changed the name of the port that metrics are collected from. The monitoring system kept looking for the old name and found nothing. From {unobserved_from} no readings arrived, and the service was still unobserved when the incident closed, {duration} later. Logs show the shop kept serving pages normally, with only ordinary client disconnects, so there is no evidence that shoppers were affected. We also cannot say for certain how the service fared, because there are no metrics for that period. Argus picked up the alert, found the likely cause, and had no safe automated mitigation for this kind of failure. It opened a draft pull request with a proposed fix and escalated to people. Argus held the incident for {held}, which measures the response and not the fault.

got_lucky: The logs suggest the service kept serving normally, but with no metrics we cannot confirm that. A real outage during this blind period would have gone undetected by metrics.
went_well: Argus took the alert up within seconds and read metrics, logs and changes together, which tied the onset to the deploy.
The Investigator separated the loss of monitoring from a service failure by reading the logs, and it did not claim an error rate it could not know.
Argus refused to take an action that did not answer the failure and escalated with a draft pull request.
went_wrong: The service was still unobserved when the incident closed, so the gap in visibility was not closed by the response.
A routine rename shipped with a scrape config left pointing at the old name.
The cause rests on an untried candidate and on timing, and was not confirmed by changing the config.

input.root_cause: The deploy at {unobserved_from} (P2) renamed the shop's metrics port from 'metrics' to 'http-metrics' as part of a naming convention, but the scrape config still selects the port by its old name. The scraper therefore lost its target and collected nothing. This rests on the Investigator's account C1, which was never tried, and on the exact match between the deploy time and the onset.
